genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure first held a junior job in a care facility
an experienced colleague pushed her to get trained
she studied in the evenings for three years before earning her diploma
she won the creation of a room set aside for expectant mothers to move about
her superiors resisted the request at first
she passed her experience on to caregivers who came from distant regions
she still runs a training session after the end of her working life
she holds that listening works as well as a drug treatment
text: The midwife at the valley clinic started out as a nursing aide. She stripped beds, wheeled carts down long corridors, and listened to women describe pains that no one took seriously. An older nurse pushed her to go back to school. She sat through evening classes and earned her certificate after three years of it. Once she joined the ward, she asked for a room where expectant mothers could walk, breathe, and doze between contractions. Her supervisors said no, then gave way. Later she trained colleagues who traveled in from far-off districts, showing them small movements no textbook had ever bothered to describe. She retired not long ago, yet she still runs a workshop where young caregivers practice listening before they reach for a prescription pad. Patience, she says, soothes as well as any carefully measured drug.

units: the most striking feature of the place is how quiet it is
an absorbing surface swallows the noise of people moving about
visitors lower their voices without being asked
the writer holds that noise breeds fatigue
fatigue sours the mood and gets in the way of falling asleep
cutting out the source of noise breaks that sequence
the writer finds the shared rooms and the kitchen dull
after two nights the muscle tension eases
text: What stays with you after a week at this rest center is not the pale architecture but the quiet it manufactures. The corridors run wide, lined with thick felt, and the material swallows footsteps so thoroughly that the ear finally lets go. The effect catches people off guard: visitors who arrive wound tight begin lowering their voices, though nobody asks them to. The reason behind it is plain, almost mechanical. Noise wears you down, weariness sours the mood, and a soured mood keeps sleep at bay. Cut the first link and the whole chain falls apart. You could fault the shared rooms for their blandness and the kitchen for playing it far too safe. Such complaints weigh little against the result: after two nights the shoulders drop, the jaw unclenches, and you catch yourself dozing in an armchair without a shred of guilt.

units: the writer blames the night cough on the state of the bedroom
the air in the room is too dry and never renewed
dryness irritates the lining of the throat and sets off a cough
he advises opening the window before going to bed
he explains that cold air, once warmed, brings moisture in
he recommends turning the heating down
he suggests setting a bowl of water near the heat source
he proposes drinking enough through the evening
he asks for a nightly note on how the symptom changes
he urges seeing a doctor if the attempt fails
text: Writing because that night cough is keeping you awake, and my hunch is that the trouble sits in your bedroom rather than in your chest. The air in there never moves: the window stays shut, the radiator runs all night, and the moisture drops below anything comfortable. A dried-out throat lining gets irritated, then answers with a hacking cough that shows up the moment you lie flat. Worth a week of trying: open the window a quarter of an hour before bed, even when it is bitter out — outside air, once it warms up indoors, carries more vapor than the stale kind. Turn the heat down a notch after that, and set a bowl of water beside it. Drink enough through the evening too, without overdoing it. Write down each night whether the cough came back. If nothing shifts, see a doctor and let me come along.

units: the question raised weighs the value of running against that of brisk walking
running puts a heavier demand on the heart within a short session
walking calls for a longer session to reach a comparable result
each running stride crushes the joints under a load greater than the person's own weight
follow-up surveys show that the gentler practice is given up less often
walking or exercise in a pool suits a damaged joint better
the writer concludes that running gives more per session and walking more across a year
text: Do you have to run to keep the heart in shape, or is brisk walking enough? It depends on what you are after. Running leans harder on the heart muscle and burns more within a short session, while a fast walk calls for a longer outing to reach the same place. The pounding, though, is another matter. Every running stride crushes the joints under a load well above the walker's own weight, and the gentler pace spares them that. Which raises a second question: which of the two do people actually keep up? Follow-up surveys point the same way every time, since the less demanding habit gets dropped less often. And what about a sore knee, or a hip that makes you limp? Caution leans toward walking, or better yet toward exercise held up by water. Per session running wins; across a year the walker does.

units: the pharmacist asks the customer when the fever began
the customer reports chills that came on the evening before
she lists a sore throat, a runny nose, sneezing and aching muscles
she admits to restless sleep and night sweats
the pharmacist marks out three priorities in what should be done
he states that an ordinary medicine is enough against a bothersome fever
he puts making up the loss of water first
he sets difficulty breathing as the signal to see a doctor
he advises rest for as long as the muscles stay tender
text: The pharmacist asked the customer how long she had been running a fever. She said the shivering had come on the evening before, out of nowhere. He wanted to know what else she felt. She listed a raw throat, a streaming nose, a constant urge to sneeze, and calves that ached. He put a question about her sleep as well; she admitted she slept badly and woke up soaked. The pharmacist then marked out three priorities. First the fever itself, which an ordinary medicine will settle whenever it bothers her. Next came fluids, which he called the urgent part, since sweating drains the reserves. Last, watchfulness: should her breathing turn difficult, a visit to a doctor becomes necessary. The customer asked whether she ought to stop moving around. He advised rest for as long as the muscles stayed tender.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: surgeons once operated without cleaning their hands
a dirty operating garment was a point of pride back then
a stubborn doctor compared the death rate of two delivery wards
deaths fell where hands were disinfected
his fellow doctors mocked him and he lost his post
research on micro-organisms brought his idea acceptance
sterilizing instruments and airing the rooms then spread
infections following operations dropped sharply
text: Picture a hospital where surgeons moved from one bed to the next without rinsing their hands, proud of the grime caked onto their aprons. That was the standard back then, and nobody saw a fault in it. Then a stubborn doctor compared two delivery wards and noticed that deaths collapsed in the one where staff scrubbed their fingers with a biting solution. His fellow doctors laughed at him, and he ended up pushed out of his post. Only the work on micro-organisms, years later, got his idea taken seriously. After that the whole thing turned over fast: instruments boiled, gowns swapped, wards aired between operations. You know the rest. Infections following surgery dropped hard, and washing your hands became the cheapest and most rewarding thing a doctor could do. Quite a reversal, wouldn't you say?

units: sitting for a long stretch makes the feet swell
the calf muscles push blood upward by squeezing the veins
staying still halts that pumping action
fluid gathers in the tissue and presses on the nerves
the pressure on the nerves accounts for the prickling feeling
heat widens the vessels and makes the whole thing worse
going short on water thickens the blood and hampers the flow
in a healthy adult the trouble normally clears after a night
staying still for a long time raises the risk of a clot forming
doctors advise standing up, tightening the calves, drinking, and keeping away from tight clothes
text: Sit still through a long trip and your feet swell while the toes go numb. The mechanism behind it is well understood. Blood climbs from the legs back toward the heart because the calf muscles squeeze the veins with every step. Stay motionless and that pump simply quits. Fluid then gathers in the tissue, the foot puffs up, and the pinched nerves send back a prickling feeling. Heat makes matters worse, since it widens the vessels. So does going short on water, because thicker blood moves less easily. In a healthy adult the whole thing stays harmless and clears after a night. The risk climbs, though, once the stillness drags on and a clot begins to take shape. Which is why doctors tell you to stand up often, tighten the calves, drink water, and keep away from clothes that grip the waist.

units: a bookbinder stayed bent over her bench through long stretches of work
a dull ache took over her forearm and then her fingers
she dropped her tool in the middle of a session
she ignored the symptom at first, taking it for something passing
the doctor she saw measured the height of the cutting surface instead of prescribing a remedy
the bench sat two hand-widths too low
the workshop was rearranged with a raised, tilted top and an adjustable seat
short breaks were brought in every half hour
the pain went away within three weeks
text: The bindery smelled of warm glue and damp paper. The binder stayed hunched over her bench through long stretches of work, wrist bent, jaw locked with concentration. A dull ache took over her forearm, then spread into her fingers, until one afternoon the folding tool slipped out of her hand mid-session. She put it down to a passing weakness and gritted her teeth. The trouble grew. A sports doctor, consulted without much hope, prescribed neither ointment nor a long rest: he measured the height of her workbench. Two hand-widths too low. They raised the top, tilted the surface, added an adjustable stool, and built in a short break every half hour. The pain went away within three weeks. She tells the story to her apprentices and laughs about it, since her ache never lived in her hands but in her furniture.

units: the choice between a cold and a warm application depends on the nature of the injury
cold suits a recent injury that comes with swelling
the ice pack must be kept off the skin by a cloth
the cold application alternates spells of a quarter of an hour
heat suits an old stiffness with no swelling
a warm water bottle is left on for half an hour
the duration must be timed with a watch and stopped if the skin turns deeply red
cold soothes and tightens while heat loosens and widens
when in doubt, cold carries fewer drawbacks
text: Before reaching for a compress, decide between cold and heat, because the two of them serve altogether different purposes. For a fresh injury, a joint that is swelling, or a knock taken the day before, go with cold. Wrap the pack in a thin cloth, hold it on for a quarter of an hour, take it off just as long, then begin the cycle over again. Never lay ice straight against the skin. For an old stiffness, a knotted neck, or a sore muscle with no swelling, heat is the better choice. A warm water bottle, left on for half an hour, loosens the fibers and frees up the movement. Either way, time it with a watch and stop once the skin turns deeply red. Keep the difference in mind: cold soothes and tightens, heat loosens and widens. When you are unsure, pick cold, which carries considerably fewer drawbacks.

the report calls for travelling clinics, dental screening among children, and marked footpaths
the health authorities will look at these proposals before the year is out
text: A health survey run across a rural area picks out three pockets of fragility. The first is diet: the adults questioned eat soft, sugary products, chew little, and show damaged teeth from middle age onward. The second concerns sleep. Nights there run short and broken by waking, which tells on alertness at the wheel and on mood. The third touches physical activity, where motorized trips have taken over from walking even across short distances. The authors point out one factor shared by all three, namely distance from care. An appointment means a long journey, one that many put off until the situation turns into an emergency. The report calls for travelling clinics, dental screening among children, and marked footpaths around the towns. The health authorities will look at these proposals before the year is out.
